For transient transfection, HEK293T cells (at ~ 70% confluency) were transfected with 10 µg DNA plasmids using X-tremeGENE 9 DNA Transfection Reagent (06365779001; Sigma-Aldrich) diluted with serum-free DMEM (41966-029; Gibco), to a concentration transfection reagent to the diluted DNA (3:1 ratio of reagent to DNA). Transient transfections were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. DNA complex was incubated for 15 min at room temperature and then the complex was added to the cells in a dropwise manner. To produce lentiviral supernatants, HEK293T cells were co-transfected with either the pLenti- AKAP2 WT_eGFP_ CMV BLASTICIDINE LUC plasmid, pMD2.G (VSVG envelope expressing plasmid) and pMDLg/pRRE, pRSV/REV (third generation lenti- viral packaging plasmids). The polyclonal cells were created through selection with blasticidin (InvivoGen).

Spheroids formation
3 × 106 Cells were seeds in low-attachment plates using ClinoStar2 bioreactor. Cells were grown for 20 days, at low-attachment conditions, in order to generate spheroids. Photo and analysis were performed with THUNDER Imager Live Cell - LEICA Microsystem, 20X of magnification.

AKAP2 is a novel ciliary protein
To elucidate the role of AKAP2 in cellular processes, we conducted a proteomic analysis of AKAP2-Flag immunopurified from HEK293T (Supplementary Fig. 1A). As shown by principal component analysis (PCA), we observed high reproducibility between three biological replicates (Supplementary Fig. 1B). Volcano plot analysis shows peptide intensity of AKAP2 interacting proteins vs. empty vector (EV) and the statistically significant interactors and ciliary proteins that specifically copurified with AKAP2 immunocomplexes (Fig. 1A). Notably, the identified interactors encompassed proteins involved in ciliary processes, actin filament remodeling, organelle localization, membrane trafficking, and cell cycle regulation (Fig. 1A and B). STRING network analysis of AKAP2 interactome revealed a pronounced enrichment of proteins implicated in cytoskeletal organization and dynamics (Fig. 1C). Consistent with the proteomic data, AKAP2 was found to bind several kinesin motor proteins, including KIF11, KIF5B, and KIF2A, along with IFT172, a key component of the intra-flagellar transport subcomplex IFT-B essential for ciliary assembly and cargo transport (Fig. 1C). Co-immunoprecipitation assays in HEK293 cells confirmed the interaction between exogenous AKAP2 and IFT172 (Fig. 1D). Additionally, AKAP2 interacted with BBS9, a component of the BBSome complex that controls intraciliary trafficking and signaling [31–33], and also with KIF2A, a ciliary-associated kinesin motor protein with microtubule-depolymerizing activity that is required for primary cilium disassembly in growth-stimulated cells [34] (Fig. 1D and E). The mitotic kinase Aurora A (AURKA) and Angiomotin (AMOT), a member of angiostatin binding proteins, were also found to interact with AKAP2 (Fig. 1D) [35–37].

Next, we sought to analyze if AKAP2 localizes within- or close to- primary cilium. To this end, we used retinal ARPE-19 cells that were growth-arrested by serum deprivation, to promote primary cilia assembly. These can be visualized by immunostaining analysis of ciliary proteins, such as Arl13b or acetylated tubulin, a modified form of tubulin that selectively accumulates within the primary cilium. As shown in Fig. 1F and G and Supplementary Fig. 2A, endogenous AKAP2 signal localizes at primary cilia, as confirmed by the co-localization with Arl13b and cilia-APEX [38], a GFP-tagged, cilia-targeted proximity labeling enzyme. Moreover, Flag- or GFP-tagged exogenous AKAP2 proteins are also localized at primary cilium (Fig. 1H and Supplementary Fig. 2B).

Molecular and functional analysis of AKAP2 knockout ARPE-19 cells
To get insight into the role of AKAP2 in cilium biology and related cellular processes, we generated AKAP2 KO ARPE-19 cells (Fig. 2A; Supplementary Fig. 3). Previous work suggested a critical role of AKAP2 in cytoskeleton events underlying cancer cell growth and motility [39, 40]. Using AKAP2 KO ARPE-19 cells, we first analyzed the impact of AKAP2 deletion on cell adhesion and migration by measuring the area, circularity and aspect ratio of focal adhesions (FAs) [41, 42], which were stained using anti-p-Paxillin antibody. In AKAP2 KO cells, we observed FAs that were larger, less circular and more elongated, indicating a significant increase of cell adhesion (Fig. 2B and C). Accordingly, while AKAP2 KO cells were overly attached to the plate surface, their migration efficiency was impaired, exhibiting slower invasion rate of a free area (wound) created in a confluent cell monolayer (Fig. 2D and E and Movie). Next, we evaluated the impact of AKAP2 deletion on cell growth by monitoring three-dimensional (3D) cell cultures formation (spheroids) of ARPE-19 cells. As shown in Fig. 2F and G downregulation of AKAP2 markedly reduced the growth of ARPE-19 spheroids, compared to controls.

To better dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying the effects of AKAP2 deletion to the retinal cell phenotype, we carried out a comparative transcriptomic analysis in control and AKAP2 KO cells. As shown in Fig. 3A, the analysis revealed 30 transcripts differentially expressed in AKAP2 KO cells, compared to wild-type cells. Hierarchical clustering of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) showed a clear separation between KO and WT samples (Fig. 3B), indicating distinct gene expression profiles driven by AKAP2 loss. Functional enrichment analysis identified pathways central to ciliary activity and retinal cell physiology, including sperm motility, glutaminergic and serotonin receptor signaling and Gap junction pathway (Fig. 3C). These pathways are known to influence retinal cell survival and neuroprotection in pathological conditions such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD) [43, 44]. The involvement of pathways like sperm motility, typically associated with cytoskeletal organization of ciliary axoneme and ATP-dependent transport, suggests that AKAP2 may influence intracellular trafficking and ARPE dynamics [45]. Interestingly, in AKAP2 KO cells, we observed downregulation of gene transcripts encoding for regulators of ciliogenesis and cilium stability, including lysophosphatidic acid (LPA) [46–48] (Fig. 3B). Additionally, AKAP2 KO cells display upregulation of transcripts encoding for regulators of primary cilium, such as neuronal regeneration-related protein (NREP) [49], serum and glucocorticoid-regulated kinase 1 (SGK1) [50], Bcl-2 interacting protein 3 (BNIP3) [51] and carbonic anhydrase gene (CA9) [52] (Fig. 3B). The analysis of upstream regulators revealed key transcription factors and signaling molecules that may significantly impact cellular processes in AKAP2 KO ARPE-19 cells. In particular, tumor necrosis factor α (TNFα), interleukin 1beta (IL1 β) and aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR) are associated with inflammatory signaling and stress responses. AKAP2 loss not only disrupts ciliary architecture, epithelial integrity, metabolic adaptation and cellular stress responses but may also trigger compensatory inflammatory pathways (Fig. 3D). Interestingly, most of identified pathways were strictly correlated with an alteration of Shh signaling [53–56].

AKAP2 is required for cilium biogenesis and Shh signaling
The data above indicates that AKAP2 localizes at primary cilium. Since AKAP2 is a PKAII specific anchor protein, we investigated the requirement of AKAP2 for PKA targeting to the cilium. In agreement with previous findings [57], immunostaining analysis of serum-deprived ARPE-19 cells confirmed that RI subunit is localized at primary cilium (Fig. 4A and B). We also found a fraction of RII subunits at ciliary compartment (Fig. 4C and D; Supplementary Fig. 4A, 4B). Interestingly, in AKAP2 KO cells, the ciliary staining of RI subunit was mostly unaffected, compared to control cells (Fig. 4A and B). In contrast, ciliary localization of RII subunits was markedly reduced by AKAP2 KO (Fig. 4C and D; Supplementary Fig. 4A, 4B). Analogous results were obtained by knockdown experiments using specific siRNAs directed against AKAP2 (Supplementary Fig. 5). Interestingly, AKAP2 KO cells also exhibit a reduced phosphorylation of PKA substrates within the primary cilium (Fig. 4E and F). Under these conditions, we did not observe major changes in the expression levels and localization of AKAP150 and GPR161, two ciliary PKA anchor proteins [21, 57], in AKAP2 KO cells (Supplementary Fig. 6). These findings indicate that AKAP2, indeed, contributes to ciliary localization and activity of PKA.

Next, we evaluated the role of AKAP2 in primary ciliogenesis. Figure 5A and B show that the number of ciliated cells was significantly reduced in AKAP2 KO cells, compared to wild type cells. Similar findings were obtained by AKAP2 knockdown using specific siRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 7C). Next, we evaluated the impact of AKAP2 deletion on ciliary trafficking. Activation of Shh pathway induces a rapid export out of cilium of G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), including the orphan receptor GPR161 [58], through a mechanism involving the BBSome complex [59, 60]. We monitored the ciliary localization of GPR161, both in control cells and in AKAP2 KO cells, under basal conditions or following Shh stimulation. As shown in Fig. 5C and D under basal conditions, AKAP2 deletion had no major effects on ciliary GPR161 staining. In wild type cells, stimulation of Shh with purmorphamine, a small agonist of the ciliary receptor Smoothened, markedly decreased the number of GPR161-positive cilia. In contrast, ligand-induced activation of Shh in AKAP2 KO cells had no major effects on the number of GPR161-positive cilia. We also analyzed the localization and trafficking of another neuronal GPCR, somatostatin receptor 3 (SSTR3), within the cilium. Following serum deprivation, cells were left untreated or stimulated with somatostatin (SST). Figure 5E and F show that, under basal conditions, no major effects in ciliary localization of SSTR3 were evident in AKAP2 KO cells, compared to wild-type cells. SST treatment induced a rapid exit of its receptor out of cilium in wild-type cells, whereas in AKAP2 KO cells the same treatment had no effects on ciliary staining of SSTR3. The effects of AKAP2 downregulation on SSTR3 and GPR161 ciliary trafficking, under basal conditions or following agonist stimulation, were replicated by genetic silencing experiments of AKAP2 (Supplementary Fig. 7A-F). Rescue experiments confirmed the role of AKAP2 in ciliary trafficking of cargo receptors. Thus, re-expressing exogenous AKAP2 (AKAP2-GFP) in AKAP2 KO cells restored the exit of endogenous GPR161 from cilium in response to Shh pathway activation, at comparable levels of wild type cells (Fig. 6A-C). Next, we analyzed whether Shh pathway activation regulates the ciliary localization of AKAP2 and PKA. As shown in Fig. 7A and B, stimulation with purmorphamine induced a rapid exit of AKAP2 out of cilium, indicating a dynamic, reversible recruitment of the anchor protein to the ciliary compartment. The exit of AKAP2 from cilium paralleled a marked decrease of ciliary PKA-RII staining (Fig. 7C and D) and a significant decrease of PKA phosphorylation of ciliary substrates (Fig. 7E and F), indicating that AKAP2 dynamically controls PKA signaling at ciliary compartment.

Given the role of AKAP2 in ciliary trafficking, we investigated whether the genetic KO of AKAP2 impacts on Shh pathway in ARPE-19 cells. Stimulation of Smoothened by its agonist removes the inhibitory constrain of PKA and promotes the exit of GLI2 factor from cilia and its consequent accumulation within the nuclear compartment (Fig. 8A). Accordingly, we evaluated the nuclear accumulation of GLI2 in control and in AKAP2 KO cells, both under basal condition or following stimulation with purmorphamine. Figure 8B and C show that AKAP2 KO cells displayed a marked impairment of Shh-induced nuclear accumulation of GLI2, compared to wild-type cells. Similar findings were obtained by AKAP2 knockdown using specific siRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 8). Immunoblot analysis of nuclear extracts from control and purmorphamine-stimulated cells confirmed that AKAP2 is, indeed, required for nuclear accumulation of GLI2 (Fig. 8D and E). Next, we evaluated the effects of AKAP2 deletion on the expression of genes required for ciliary morphogenesis and trafficking. Figure 8F and G show that genetic deletion of AKAP2 induced a marked reduction of mRNAs encoding for ciliary genes. AKAP2 controls cilium development in Medaka fish
To further investigate the role of AKAP2 in ciliogenesis, we conducted an in vivo analysis using the Medaka fish (Oryzias latipes, ol). We generated a GFP-tagged wild-type AKAP2 construct and two AKAP2-GFP mutants carrying alanine substitutions of key residues within the actin-binding domain that destroy the interaction to actin cytoskeleton (AKAP2 F-Mutant) [40] or substitutions of two alanine residues to proline within the RII binding domain (AKAP2 RII-Mutant) [61] that affects PKAII binding to AKAP2 (Fig. 9A). First, we analyzed the expression and ciliary distribution of olAKAP2 in Medaka fish. As shown in Fig. 9B, we confirmed the localization of endogenous olAKAP2 at primary cilium in vivo. Next, we assessed the ciliary localization of GFP-tagged AKAP2 constructs. Figure 9B shows that both AKAP2 F-Mut and AKAP2 RII mutants were not localized at the cilia, compared to the wild-type AKAP2, indicating that the binding to PKA and/or actin is a prerequisite for AKAP2 targeting to ciliary compartment. Next, we evaluated the impact of olAkap2 downregulation on Medaka fish development and ciliogenesis by performing genetic silencing experiments using a morpholino (Mo, Gene Tools) targeting the olAkap2 transcript. The efficiency and specificity of AKAP2 knock-down were verified using appropriate controls [62]. The depletion of olAkap2 caused a delay in embryonic development, resulting in a significant increased embryonic death rate (~ 60%) (Fig. 9C and D). As expected, the injection of Mo-AKAP2 along with AKAP2 mRNA was able to rescue the observed phenotype, confirming the role of AKAP2 in Medaka fish development (Fig. 9C and D). To verify the specificity of AKAP2 mRNA, we also tested the effects of a single mRNA injection on Medaka fish phenotype. As highlighted, injecting AKAP2 mRNA alone did not change the embryo phenotype. Next, we evaluated whether overexpression of mutant forms of AKAP2 mRNAs may induce possible changes in cilia development. Indeed, injections of AKAP2 F-Mut and AKAP2 RII-Mut resulted in alterations of embryo development and embryonic death rate (Fig. 9C and D). Consistently, co-injections of mutant forms of AKAP2 mRNAs with MoAkap2 could not rescue morphological embryo defects (Fig. 9C). However, we observed an amelioration of the embryo survival (Fig. 9D). To evaluate if the observed MoAKAP2 phenotype was related to ciliogenesis defects, we measured the cilia length on cell surface of neural tube of Medaka embryos at stage 24 through whole-mount immunofluorescence with anti-acetylated α-tubulin. As shown in Fig. 9E and G and Supplementary Fig. 9, we detected a significant reduction in cilia length in MoAKAP2 morphant embryos. Consistently, the co-injection of AKAP2 mRNA with MoAKAP2 significantly rescued cilia development (Fig. 9F and G). In contrast, injections of AKAP2 F-Mut and AKAP2-RII Mut resulted in a significant defect in cilia growth (Fig. 9F). Moreover, co-injections of the mutated forms of AKAP2 gene with MoAkap2 could not rescue ciliogenesis (Fig. 9F and G). These data strongly support that the binding of AKAP2 to PKA and actin are both required for cilium biogenesis, signaling and Medaka fish development. To further assess the role of ol-Akap2, we also analyzed the localization and trafficking of both SSTR3 and GPR161 receptors in the cilium. In agreement with the in vitro data, under basal conditions, both receptors had a ciliary localization in wild-type and Mo-Akap2 embryos. Following agonist stimulation, we observed a rapid exit of both receptors from the ciliary compartment only in wild-type embryos, whereas no major effects were observed in Mo-Akap2 embryos. (Fig. 10A-D). Consistently, rescue experiments consolidated the requirement of AKAP2 for proper ciliary trafficking of the cargo receptors. Thus, reintroduction of exogenous AKAP2 into AKAP2‑depleted embryos reinstated the ability of both endogenous SSTR3 and GPR161 to exit the cilium under stimulations with SST and purmorphamine, respectively (Fig. 10A-D).

Discussion
Here, we provide evidence of the existence of a scaffold complex assembled by AKAP2 at primary cilium that controls different aspects of cilium biology. Specifically, we found that AKAP2 expression and localization at primary cilium are required for ciliogenesis, ciliary trafficking of G protein-coupled receptors, and Shh signaling (Fig. 11). Genetic downregulation of AKAP2 in retinal epithelial cells markedly affected ciliogenesis and signaling. The role of AKAP2 in primary cilium activities has been confirmed by manipulating olAKAP2 expression in Medaka fish. Here, genetic knockdown of AKAP2 causes ciliary defects associated with a significant delay in embryonic development and an increase rate of embryonic lethality. Rescue experiments demonstrated the requirement of PKA- and actin-binding properties of AKAP2 in mediating the physiological events underlying embryos development and survival.

Fig. 11AKAP2 regulates Sonic hedgehog signaling cascade at the ciliary compartment. In absence of Shh ligand (Shh off), the receptor Patched1 (Ptch1) inhibits Smoothened (SMO) signaling. AKAP2 binds to the IFT complex and localizes PKAII at the ciliary compartment. GPR161 activates adenylyl cyclase (AC), thus increasing cAMP levels that induce activation of AKAP2-bound PKAII that, in turns, represses Gli transcription factor. The binding of Shh ligand (Shh on), induces the exit of Ptch1 from the ciliary compartment and the consequent translocation of SMO within the cilium, that represses AC. The inhibition of AC, results in the export of AKAP2, PKAII and GPR161 from the cilium and in the translocation of Gli2 to the nucleus, promoting the Shh-dependent gene transcription

Primary cilium acts as a central hub that coordinates distinct signaling events underlying many cellular activities regulating differentiation, growth, metabolism, and survival. cAMP mediates the biological responses of cells to stimulation of specific GPCRs by dedicated hormones and neurotransmitters. The rise of cAMP levels within the primary cilium by a GPR161-mediated activation of ciliary adenylate cyclase maintains an inhibitory loop on Shh signaling pathway, preventing basal activation of GLI2 transcription factor and downstream GLI2-dependent gene transcription [16, 19, 57, 63]. GPR161 acts as an AKAP that recruits PKAI to primary cilium and regulates PKA-dependent Shh pathway [57]. Evidence indicates that Smoothened uses a decoy substrate sequence that interacts with catalytic subunit of PKA [64], thereby restraining its activity and promoting the release of GLI2 inhibition and consequent activation of downstream Shh pathway [64]. The novelty of our study relies on the identification of AKAP2 as a ciliary protein with important roles in targeting PKAII to the ciliary compartment and regulating Shh pathway, contributing to a significant share of total PKA activity at ciliary compartment. Thus, genetic deletion of AKAP2 markedly reduced the localization of RII subunits of PKA at ciliary compartment, with no major effects on ciliary RI subunits. This is consistent with previous findings indicating that AKAP2 is a PKAII-specific AKAP [65]. Interestingly, we also found that the localization of AKAP2 and PKAII at ciliary compartment is highly dynamic. Thus, following activation of Shh pathway, both AKAP2 and PKA-RII are rapidly exported out of cilium, and this event is linked to a significant downregulation of PKA phosphorylation of ciliary substrates. This represents a unique mechanism to dynamically and reversibly convey cAMP signals to a discrete compartment, with major biological effects on downstream PKA targets. However, the identity and functional role of ciliary PKA substrates, as well as the contribution of additional AKAPs AKAPs to ciliary PKA activity, await further characterization.

The role of AKAP2 in cilium biogenesis and ciliary activities is supported by the identification of a de novo translocation t(7;9)(p14.1;q31.3) on chromosome 9 that disrupts the AKAP2 gene in a patient affected by Kallmann syndrome (KS) [66]. This is a ciliopathy disorder characterized by congenital bone anomalies, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH) due to gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) deficiency, anosmia or hyposmia, involuntary mirror movements, dental irregularities, kidney-related complications, midline facial anomalies, hearing impairment, and defects in eye movement [67, 68]. However, the pathogenic role of AKAP2 deletion in KS needs further investigation.

AKAP2 controls several aspects of actin cytoskeleton, being implicated in cell motility, cancer invasion and mitogenic pathways [40, 69–71]. AKAP2 is overexpressed in a variety of epithelial cancer cells and its levels positively correlate with the malignant phenotype and invasiveness potential of cancer cells [39, 40, 72, 73]. AKAP2 undergoes to mitotic degradation through a PLK1/βTrCP-signaling pathway and its proteolysis is required for proper cell cycle progression [74]. Here, we added another layer of complexity in the biological functions of this anchor protein by demonstrating that ciliary localization of AKAP2 in growth-arrested cells is a prerequisite for cilium biogenesis and trafficking. Accordingly, downregulation of AKAP2 in retinal cells impaired the sorting out of GPCRs from cilium in response to Shh pathway activation, indicating that AKAP2 is a sensor and regulator of Shh pathway. Given the role of Shh in different aspects of cancer cell growth and progression, by modulating GLI2-dependent gene transcription, AKAP2 may act as a positive regulator of cancer development [75].

Studies in Medaka fish model confirmed the localization and the role of AKAP2 at primary cilium and implicated the actin- and PKA-binding domains for ciliary localization of the protein. In this model system, AKAP2 silencing significantly affected ciliogenesis, embryo development and survival. Importantly, AKAP2 depletion in the medaka model leads to a clear defect in cilia development, manifested as shorter cilia development rather than a complete loss of cilia. The apparent divergence between the in vivo phenotype and the in vitro observations might reflect biological differences between the two systems rather than a discrepancy in AKAP2 function. In the in vivo medaka context, cilia assemble within a fully polarized, three‑dimensional epithelium, where AKAP2 loss impacts both the initiation of ciliogenesis and the subsequent elongation and maintenance. Conversely, the cell‑based assays are performed in two‑dimensional culture, where cilia extend into an unconstrained environment and exhibit greater intrinsic variability in length. In this setting, AKAP2 depletion primarily compromises ciliogenesis initiation, resulting in a reduced proportion of ciliated cells rather than a consistent shortening of those cilia that do form.

The developmental defects observed in AKAP2-silenced Medaka fish embryos were fully rescued by re-expressing AKAP2 wild type, but not AKAP2 mutants lacking the PKA- or actin-binding activity. Interestingly, both AKAP2 mutants failed to localize at ciliary compartment. The binding of AKAP2 to actin is required to localize the protein at the actin cytoskeleton [40, 76]. Given the actin-based structure of the ciliary axoneme, the actin-binding property of AKAP2 is, indeed, a prerequisite for its localization at primary cilium. We also demonstrate that the binding of PKA to AKAP2 regulates ciliary localization of the protein. This most likely involves the interaction of AKAP2-bound PKA to components of the ciliary compartment, as previously reported [64]. These data suggest that AKAP2 by interacting with PKA and with components of the ciliary cytoskeleton acts as a key signaling node for ciliary trafficking and Shh pathway, regulating both the formation and elongation of primary cilium. The identification of additional AKAP2 partners and the mechanisms underlying the recruitment of AKAP2 at primary cilium will further contribute to the dynamic interplay between compartmentalized cAMP signaling and cilium biology.

In summary, our findings reveal a key role of AKAP2 in cilium biology. The dynamic localization of AKAP2 and PKAII at primary cilium, and its role in ciliary trafficking and signaling represent important steps forward our understanding of the mechanisms regulating ciliary-based PKA pathways. Manipulating this regulatory circuitry may, thus, subserve as a therapeutic option for the treatment of proliferative and developmental disorders.

paper.title: Ductular reaction as a spatial fibrogenic niche: cholangiocyte-macrophage-fibroblast crosstalk in chronic liver disease.
paper.abstract: Ductular reaction-the expansion of reactive bile ductules at the portal-parenchymal interface-has traditionally been interpreted as a proliferative or regenerative response of the biliary epithelium to chronic injury. Here we argue that this histological phenomenon is better understood as a spatial fibrogenic niche: a physically organized, self-reinforcing microenvironment in which reactive cholangiocytes, macrophages, and matrix-producing mesenchymal cells engage in bidirectional signaling that converts repair into fibrosis. We integrate single-cell and spatial transcriptomic evidence showing that reactive cholangiocytes act as a signaling hub, secreting TGF-β, PDGF, CCL2, CXCL chemokines, IL-6, osteopontin, and Hedgehog ligands; that recruited and tissue-resident macrophages amplify this axis; and that portal fibroblasts and hepatic stellate cells close a feed-forward loop by depositing extracellular matrix and growth factors that sustain the niche. We propose that a cholangiocyte-macrophage-fibroblast feed-forward loop, stabilized by chemokine-driven recruitment, TGF-β-centered fibrogenesis, mechanical feedback, and senescence, underlies ductular-associated fibrosis across cholestatic and metabolic liver diseases. Targeting the pathological organization of this niche-rather than any single cell type-may offer a new therapeutic framework for chronic liver fibrosis.
paper.full_text:
Introduction
Ductular reaction—the expansion of reactive bile ductules at the interface between the portal tract and the hepatic parenchyma—is among the most common and reproducible histological findings in chronic liver disease. It is observed in cholestatic disorders, including primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), and biliary atresia, but it is equally prominent in parenchymal injury of metabolic, alcoholic, and viral etiology (1, 2). Identified by cytokeratin 7 (CK7), cytokeratin 19 (CK19), SOX9, and EpCAM, the reaction expands reactive biliary cells together with a surrounding inflammatory and mesenchymal cuff, and its extent has long served as a histological surrogate of disease activity and fibrosis stage (1, 2). The near-universality of ductular reaction across etiologically distinct diseases is itself a clue that it reflects a shared, fundamental response of the liver to chronic injury rather than a disease-specific epiphenomenon.

Traditionally, ductular reaction has been interpreted primarily as a proliferative or regenerative response of the biliary epithelium—an attempt by the liver to replenish damaged bile ducts and, in severe injury, to supply hepatocytes through the activation of hepatic progenitor-like cells (3). This regenerative reading is attractive, and it is certainly part of the story: ductular cells are bipotential in many models and can contribute to parenchymal restoration. It is, however, incomplete. A substantial body of evidence now indicates that ductular reaction is not a uniform epithelial compartment but a spatially organized assembly of reactive cholangiocytes, macrophages, portal fibroblasts, hepatic stellate cells, endothelial cells, and extracellular matrix (ECM), whose coordinated signaling actively drives—rather than merely accompanies—fibrogenesis (4–6). Correlatively, the magnitude of ductular reaction tracks fibrosis stage and adverse outcomes across diseases, even where it was once dismissed as a passive bystander of scarring (7).

This review proposes a “ductular reaction-associated spatial fibrogenic niche” framework. We synthesize evidence that reactive cholangiocytes operate as the signaling hub of this niche, that macrophages amplify ductular fibrogenesis, and that fibroblasts and hepatic stellate cells provide the matrix-producing arm, and we argue that the spatiotemporal interplay among these three compartments—rather than any one cell type in isolation—constitutes the engine of chronic hepatic fibrosis. We then consider how this niche manifests in specific diseases, how emerging spatial technologies are redefining it, and how targeting its organization, rather than its individual cells, might yield new antifibrotic strategies. The overall conceptual framework of the ductular reaction-associated spatial fibrogenic niche, including the transition from adaptive repair to progressive fibrosis, is summarized in Figure 1.

Ductular reaction: from histological phenomenon to dynamic fibrogenic niche
Ductular reaction denotes the expansion of reactive bile ductules and their associated cellular constituents at the portal–parenchymal interface in response to liver injury (1). Histologically it encompasses a spectrum, from simple proliferation of pre-existing bile ductules to the appearance of atypical, frequently irregular and anastomosing tubular structures lined by cells that co-express biliary (CK7, CK19, SOX9, EpCAM) and progenitor markers (8). This morphological spectrum reflects underlying biological heterogeneity: some ductular profiles represent genuine regenerative attempts, whereas others are disorganized, non-functional structures that fail to reconnect the biliary tree and instead accumulate within an expanding scar (1, 2). The reaction is invariably accompanied by periductular inflammation, deposition of ECM, and expansion of a loose mesenchymal cuff of activated fibroblasts—features that already hint at its intimate coupling to fibrogenesis (2).

Ductular reaction is a near-universal feature of chronic liver disease, but its prominence and character differ by etiology. It is most florid in cholestatic conditions—PSC, PBC, and biliary atresia—where cholangiocyte injury is the primary insult (1, 2). It is also prominent, however, in advanced metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), alcohol-associated liver disease, and chronic viral hepatitis, where it emerges late and tracks the transition to bridging fibrosis (7). This cross-etiology convergence is important for the argument developed here: if the same reactive biliary structures appear in diseases whose primary insults are so different—autoimmune, cholestatic, metabolic, toxic, and viral—then the biology they share is likely to reside not in the initial injury but in a conserved downstream program of multicellular interaction.

The cellular sources of ductular reaction have been intensely debated, and three contributors are consistently supported. First, resident cholangiocytes proliferate and acquire a reactive phenotype in response to biliary injury. Second, hepatic progenitor-like cells—the oval cells of rodents—residing within the canals of Hering expand bipotentially when hepatocyte replication is impaired. Third, mature hepatocytes can transdifferentiate toward a biliary fate through hepatocyte-to-biliary plasticity, a process dependent on Notch and Hippo/YAP signaling that is particularly prominent in biliary-dominant injury (3, 9, 10). The relative contribution of each source varies by disease context, species, and injury severity, and this cell-of-origin question remains unresolved. We deliberately do not adjudicate it here, because it does not materially change the niche argument: whatever their origin, the epithelial cells of the ductular reaction converge on a shared reactive, secretory, pro-fibrotic phenotype that organizes the surrounding microenvironment.

The central proposition of this review is that ductular reaction is not a pure epithelial phenomenon but a spatial niche. Reactive cholangiocytes are not surrounded by a single cell type; they are encircled by a stereotyped ensemble of macrophages, portal fibroblasts, hepatic stellate cells, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, and a growing ECM scaffold (4–6). This is not a loose association but a structured neighborhood. Spatial profiling has shown that these cells are organized into periductular zones with defined gradients of signaling molecules and matrix components, and that specific cell states—scar-associated macrophages, activated myofibroblasts, and reactive cholangiocytes—are reproducibly co-localized around the same ductular profiles (5).

Why does this spatial organization matter, rather than merely the presence of these cells somewhere in the liver? Because proximity is functional. Confining ligands and their receptors to a narrow periductular band concentrates signaling, enforces cell–cell contact, and creates mechanical constraints that feed back onto gene expression through integrins and mechanosensitive pathways. A cholangiocyte that secretes CCL2, a monocyte that follows that gradient, and a fibroblast that stiffens the local matrix are each individually unremarkable; placed within tens of micrometers of one another, they constitute a self-reinforcing circuit. We therefore propose that the ductular reaction-associated niche—defined by the spatial co-organization of reactive cholangiocytes, immune cells, mesenchymal cells, and ECM—is the functional unit through which chronic injury is translated into fibrosis.

Reactive cholangiocytes as the signaling hub of the fibrogenic niche
Reactive cholangiocytes are far more than hyperplastic bile-duct cells. Under chronic injury they undergo a profound phenotypic remodeling that encompasses proliferation, a neuroendocrine and secretory phenotype, upregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines, and—critically—entry into senescence (6, 11). This remodeling is graded. Mild, transient injury elicits an adaptive, proliferative response that restores epithelial integrity and then resolves. Persistent injury, by contrast, drives an inflammatory, senescent, and secretory state that is intrinsically pro-fibrotic and that no longer serves a reparative function (1). The reactive cholangiocyte is therefore best characterized not by a single marker but by a constellation of proliferation, senescence, inflammation, and secretion—and it is this constellation, rather than proliferation alone, that defines its role in the niche.

The functional consequence of this remodeling is that reactive cholangiocytes become a dominant source of fibrogenic and chemotactic signals, acting on every other cellular compartment within the periductular space. Several classical pathways stand out. Reactive cholangiocytes secrete TGF-β—notably the TGF-β2 isoform—a master driver of mesenchymal activation that acts directly on portal fibroblasts and hepatic stellate cells (1, 6). They secrete PDGF, in particular PDGF-BB, which recruits and activates those same mesenchymal cells and promotes their proliferation and migration (1). They secrete CCL2 (MCP-1), the principal monocyte chemoattractant of the injured liver, together with a panel of CXCL chemokines that broaden the inflammatory infiltrate (12). They secrete IL-6, which in autocrine fashion sustains cholangiocyte proliferation and in paracrine fashion promotes inflammation (1). They secrete osteopontin (SPP1), which polarizes macrophages toward a pro-fibrotic phenotype (13). And they secrete Hedgehog ligands—Shh and Ihh—which activate a dedicated population of peribiliary mesenchymal cells (14, 15). Together, this secretory program supports a central organizing role for reactive cholangiocytes in initiating and sustaining the niche's inflammatory and fibrogenic signaling.

The Hedgehog axis deserves emphasis because it is one of the clearest demonstrations that cholangiocyte-derived signals are spatially targeted rather than diffuse. In biliary injury, Hedgehog-responsive peribiliary mesenchymal cells accumulate precisely around reactive ductules, and genetic or pharmacologic inhibition of the pathway attenuates biliary fibrosis (14, 15). This is, in essence, a niche-specific ligand–receptor system: the cholangiocyte produces the ligand, and a dedicated mesenchymal responder that resides immediately adjacent to it transduces the signal into matrix production.

These observations connect repair directly to fibrosis through a transition that we regard as pivotal: adaptive regeneration → persistent injury → maladaptive ductular reaction → fibrosis. In its adaptive phase, ductular reaction restores biliary continuity and is self-limiting. When injury persists, the same program fails to resolve: cholangiocytes remain locked in a proliferative-secretory state, continue to emit fibrogenic and chemotactic signals, and recruit a self-perpetuating inflammatory–mesenchymal response (1, 6). Cholangiocyte-intrinsic signaling such as the non-canonical NF-κB mediator NIK directly sustains ductular reaction and fibrosis, indicating that the epithelial compartment itself drives, rather than merely reports, the fibrogenic program (16). The ductular reaction thereby converts from a repair structure into a fibrogenic niche—a conceptual shift, from “reaction” as outcome to “niche” as driver, that is central to our framework.

Macrophages as amplifiers of ductular fibrogenesis
Hepatic macrophages comprise two broad populations whose origins, maintenance, and functions differ. Resident Kupffer cells arise from embryonic precursors and self-renew locally, whereas monocyte-derived macrophages are recruited from circulating Ly6C-high monocytes through the CCL2–CCR2 and CSF1 axes during injury (17, 18). This distinction is not merely academic: it maps onto divergent roles. In chronic injury the monocyte-derived compartment expands substantially and becomes the principal source of pro-fibrotic mediators, while Kupffer cells can also contribute—particularly in cholestatic contexts, where they are positioned at the biliary interface (18, 19). The balance between these populations, and their phenotypic conversion upon entering the niche, is a major determinant of whether injury resolves or progresses.

Communication between cholangiocytes and macrophages is bidirectional and central to niche amplification. Reactive cholangiocytes recruit macrophages by secreting CCL2 and CSF1, thereby initiating the immune arm of the niche (12, 20). In return, macrophages release TGF-β, TNF, IL-1β, PDGF, and osteopontin, which further stimulate ductular reaction and fibroblast activation (13, 19). This creates a self-amplifying loop in which the cholangiocyte summons the very cells that will drive its own reactive phenotype and the surrounding fibrogenesis. The macrophage is therefore not a bystander but an amplifier of ductular fibrogenesis.

A particularly compelling illustration comes from osteopontin. Bile-duct-associated macrophages that express osteopontin are enriched in fibrotic cholestatic livers and correlate with fibrosis, suggesting that a distinct macrophage population is anatomically and functionally tethered to the biliary niche (13). Because osteopontin itself promotes macrophage recruitment and polarization and has been implicated across a broad range of chronic liver diseases, it exemplifies a niche-reinforcing factor that operates at multiple nodes of the loop (13, 21).

Single-cell studies have resolved macrophages into dynamically changing states that map onto disease progression. In fibrotic human cirrhosis, scar-associated macrophages (SAMacs)—marked by TREM2 and CD9—accumulate within the fibrotic niche and express pro-fibrotic factors (4). Related TREM2-positive lipid-associated macrophages (22) and CD9-positive macrophages define conserved niches across human liver disease (5). An inflammatory, monocyte-derived macrophage population predominates in early steatohepatitis, whereas a more restorative or scar-associated phenotype accumulates as fibrosis advances (18, 21). These state transitions—from inflammatory to scar-associated—provide a molecular timeline linking macrophage phenotype to niche evolution, and they suggest that the niche does not merely accumulate macrophages but actively reprograms them.

Fibroblasts and hepatic stellate cells as the matrix-producing arm
Portal fibroblasts are the principal mesenchymal population associated with the ductular reaction in cholestatic disease. They reside in the portal mesenchyme and are activated early in biliary injury, where they differentiate into collagen-producing myofibroblasts (23). They are distinguished from hepatic stellate cells by markers including elastin, fibulin-2, and thy-1, and—importantly—a subset with mesenchymal stem cell features appears to constitute a reservoir of proliferative myofibroblasts in biliary fibrosis (23). This positions portal fibroblasts as the matrix-producing arm most tightly coupled to the periductular niche, and it explains why biliary fibrosis classically begins as periductular, concentric scarring rather than as the sinusoidal fibrosis typical of parenchymal disease.

Hepatic stellate cells (HSCs), by contrast, are the dominant myofibroblast source in chronic parenchymal injury of metabolic, alcoholic, and viral etiology (24, 25). Upon activation, quiescent vitamin A-storing HSCs transdifferentiate into α-SMA-positive myofibroblasts that deposit fibrillar ECM and secrete growth factors (26). Although classically associated with sinusoidal injury, HSCs also contribute to portal and bridging fibrosis, and their activation is intimately linked to the inflammatory milieu of the ductular niche (24). The two mesenchymal lineages are therefore not mutually exclusive but complementary: portal fibroblasts dominate the biliary and periductular compartment, and HSCs dominate the sinusoidal and septal compartment, with both converging on the same activated myofibroblast effector program in advanced disease.

Single-cell transcriptomics has dissolved the notion of a homogeneous “fibroblast.” Analyses of human and murine liver reveal distinct portal fibroblast subsets, a continuum of activated myofibroblasts, and specialized scar-associated mesenchymal populations, with functionally opposing HSC subpopulations distinguished in hepatocarcinogenesis (27–29). This heterogeneity carries a functional implication for the niche concept: different mesenchymal subsets serve different niches, and therapeutic strategies that target “fibroblasts” as a single entity are likely to miss the subset that actually sustains a given periductular lesion.

The cholangiocyte–fibroblast axis closes a genuine positive-feedback loop. Reactive cholangiocytes activate fibroblasts through TGF-β, PDGF, and Hedgehog ligands, inducing collagen production (1, 15). In return, fibroblasts deposit ECM and secrete growth factors that sustain cholangiocyte proliferation and the reactive phenotype, physically embedding the ductular cells in a stiffening, pro-inflammatory matrix (1, 30). This bidirectionality is the mechanistic core of the niche concept: neither compartment persists in its pathological state without the other.

Together, these three sections establish the cast of the niche: a cholangiocyte hub that emits fibrogenic and chemotactic signals, a macrophage amplifier that reprograms in response to those signals, and a mesenchymal effector arm that converts the signals into matrix and, in turn, sustains the epithelial and immune compartments. Table 1 summarizes the defining markers, cell states, and functional contributions of the cellular compartments of the niche. What remains is to explain how these three actors are wired into a single self-reinforcing circuit—the subject of the next section.

Building the spatial fibrogenic niche: multicellular crosstalk and feed-forward loops
The preceding sections describe the three actors separately; here we reassemble them. We propose that the niche is sustained by a triangular, self-reinforcing loop—reactive cholangiocyte ↔ macrophage ↔ fibroblast ↔ reactive cholangiocyte—that we term the cholangiocyte–macrophage–fibroblast feed-forward loop. The loop has several separable but interlocking components, which we dissect in turn.

Chemokine-mediated inflammatory recruitment initiates and maintains the loop. Reactive cholangiocytes secrete CCL2 and CXCL chemokines that recruit monocytes and other inflammatory cells into the periductular space (1, 12). Recruited monocytes differentiate into pro-fibrotic macrophages that in turn secrete additional chemokines, sustaining recruitment and reinforcing the niche's inflammatory tone (17, 18). Recruitment is thus not a one-time event but a self-perpetuating process that keeps the niche continuously populated with effector cells.

TGF-β-centered fibrogenic signaling sits at the center of the loop. Produced by both reactive cholangiocytes and recruited macrophages, TGF-β activates portal fibroblasts and HSCs to produce ECM and further TGF-β, creating a fibrogenic auto-induction circuit (6, 25, 26). TGF-β also directly sustains cholangiocyte proliferation and epithelial–mesenchymal-transition-like changes in biliary injury (14). The convergence of epithelial- and macrophage-derived TGF-β on the same mesenchymal targets—together with the latent TGF-β reservoir embedded in the newly deposited matrix—is a hallmark of the niche and a reason it is difficult to interrupt with single-agent blockade.

ECM remodeling and mechanical feedback make the matrix an active participant rather than an inert output. Fibroblast-deposited collagen and laminin stiffen the periductular stroma, and this altered mechanical environment may engage integrin-dependent mechanotransduction pathways, including context-dependent YAP/TAZ signaling, in cholangiocytes and mesenchymal cells (31). Integrin αvβ6 on injured epithelium can activate latent TGF-β1, providing a mechanistic link between matrix adhesion and fibrogenic signaling (32); however, the magnitude and cell-type specificity of these pathways in the ductular niche remain to be defined. The niche may therefore acquire a form of mechanical memory in which matrix stiffening helps sustain the signaling environment that produced it.

Senescence and SASP-mediated niche stabilization convert a potentially reversible response into a persistent one. Senescent cholangiocytes—prominent in cholestatic disease—secrete a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) of pro-inflammatory and pro-fibrotic factors that sustains inflammation and fibrosis (11, 33). Senescent and p21-positive TREM2-positive macrophage populations similarly reinforce the niche, and the SASP provides a mechanistic link between chronic injury and the persistence of fibrogenesis even after the initial insult recedes (34).

Vascular and metabolic contributions support, but do not dominate, the niche. Liver sinusoidal endothelial cells undergo capillarization and gate the inflammatory response, and laminin deposition by endothelial cells shapes cholangiocyte fate (35, 36). Local hypoxia and bile-acid accumulation further condition the niche, promoting cholangiocyte proliferation and inflammation (6). We treat these inputs as contextual amplifiers rather than core drivers: they tune the set-point of the loop, but the loop itself is defined by the epithelial–immune–mesenchymal interactions described above. Table 2 summarizes the principal intercellular signaling axes of the niche, specifying the source and target cell for each and its effect within the feed-forward loop.

Disease-specific manifestations of the ductular fibrogenic niche
Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is the paradigm of a ductular fibrogenic niche. The disease features concentric peribiliary fibrosis (“onion-skinning”), a florid ductular reaction, and prominent cholangiocyte senescence, all organized around inflamed bile ducts (37, 38). Cholangiocyte-derived chemokines such as CCL24 have been directly implicated in PSC-associated biliary fibrosis, and single-cell and spatial analyses reveal a periductal niche enriched in reactive cholangiocytes, T cells, and scar-associated macrophages (39, 40). PSC thus exemplifies how an epithelial injury response is organized—literally, in concentric rings—into a niche that drives the signature fibrosis of the disease.

Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) illustrates a complementary facet. In PBC, autoimmune-mediated cholangiocyte injury and apoptosis drive ductopenia, yet this is accompanied by a ductular reaction that correlates with fibrosis (39, 41). Cholangiocyte senescence is a defining feature, and the SASP is thought to perpetuate portal inflammation and fibrosis even as the biliary tree is progressively depleted (11, 33). PBC therefore demonstrates that cholangiocyte loss and reactive proliferation coexist, and that the surviving reactive cholangiocytes continue to generate a fibrogenic niche even while the total biliary epithelium shrinks—a dissociation between regeneration and fibrosis that underscores the maladaptive nature of the niche.

Biliary atresia extends the niche concept to the neonatal liver. This cholangiopathy features a progressive inflammatory obliteration of the extrahepatic bile ducts, accompanied by an exuberant intrahepatic ductular reaction and rapid biliary fibrosis (42, 43). The speed and intensity with which the niche is established in infants—where epithelial injury, immune activation, and mesenchymal response coincide in a still-developing liver—reinforce that the fibrogenic niche is not a late-stage phenomenon unique to adult disease but a general and rapidly inducible program.

Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is particularly instructive because it demonstrates that the niche is not restricted to cholestatic disease. In MASH, ductular reaction emerges as fibrosis advances and is now recognized as a key correlate of fibrogenesis rather than an incidental finding (1, 7). Single-cell and spatial studies map TREM2-positive and CD9-positive macrophages and activated HSCs around reactive ductules in steatohepatitic fibrosis (4, 5, 21). The convergence of metabolic injury, macrophage accumulation, and ductular reaction in MASH suggests that, once a certain threshold of chronic injury is crossed, the same spatial niche assembles regardless of whether the primary insult is biliary or metabolic.

Alcohol-associated liver disease and chronic viral hepatitis complete the spectrum. Here ductular reaction appears in advanced fibrotic and cirrhotic stages, where the periductular niche merges with broad bridging fibrosis (1, 7). While less cholangiocyte-centric than PSC and PBC, these diseases share the same terminal niche architecture—reactive ductules, scar-associated macrophages, and activated myofibroblasts—supporting the generality of the framework (4). Table 3 summarizes these disease-specific manifestations, including the primary insult, defining niche features, and characteristic fibrosis pattern in each condition.

Across these diseases, the niche is therefore expressed in graded fashion: a cholangiocyte-dominant niche in PSC and PBC, an early and rapid niche in biliary atresia, and a late-assembling niche in MASH and alcoholic/viral disease. This disease-specific variation is itself informative—it suggests that the niche is a conserved downstream program whose tempo and cellular emphasis are set by the primary insult, a point we return to when considering the outstanding questions.

Spatial omics and emerging technologies redefining the ductular niche
The recent reconceptualization of ductular reaction owes much to single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). This technology has resolved the cellular composition of the fibrotic niche and its dynamic states—reactive cholangiocytes, macrophage subsets, and mesenchymal heterogeneity—across human liver disease (4, 21, 29). It established that the niche is a composite of transcriptionally distinct cell states, not a single pathological cell type, and it supplied the first unbiased catalogs of the ligands and receptors that these states express.

Spatial transcriptomics adds the positional information that scRNA-seq discards. Technologies such as Visium and MERFISH reveal that the relevant cell states are physically co-localized in periductular and portal zones, and studies of healthy and fibrotic human liver at single-cell resolution have mapped reactive cholangiocytes and scar-associated macrophages into defined spatial neighborhoods (5, 18, 44). This is the decisive step for the niche concept: it shows not merely that a cell state exists, but that it occupies a specific position relative to others.

Multiplex imaging platforms—CODEX, imaging mass cytometry, and multiplex immunofluorescence—extend this resolution to the protein level, validating ligand–receptor co-localization and cell-neighborhood architecture in situ (5). These tools confirm that the molecular interactions inferred computationally occur at actual cell–cell contacts, closing the gap between predicted and observed communication.

Reductionist systems complement these observational maps. Cholangiocyte organoids recapitulate reactive cholangiocyte biology and can even repair bile ducts after transplantation, while branching organoid and liver-on-chip models reconstruct periportal architecture and biliary fibrosis in vitro (45, 46). These systems allow causal interrogation of niche interactions—perturbing one compartment and observing the response of the others—something observational omics cannot resolve.

Finally, integrative computational approaches—ligand–receptor analysis, cell–cell communication inference, and niche-detection algorithms—transform these datasets into testable models of interaction (5, 21). The field has thereby moved from asking “who expresses what” to asking “who communicates with whom, and where.” That positional-communication question is, in essence, the spatial-niche concept made operational.

Therapeutic opportunities: targeting the ductular fibrogenic niche
If the niche—rather than any single cell type—sustains ductular-associated fibrosis, then the therapeutic goal shifts from eliminating a cell population to disrupting the niche's organization and signaling. We frame the emerging opportunities accordingly.

Targeting reactive cholangiocytes. Modulating the reactive cholangiocyte phenotype—its proliferation, senescence, and secretome—could de-escalate the niche at its hub (6, 11). Senolytic approaches have emerged as a potential strategy for reducing senescence-associated signaling, although their efficacy and selectivity toward senescent cholangiocytes in chronic liver disease remain to be established (34). The challenge is to blunt the maladaptive phenotype without abolishing the regenerative capacity of the biliary epithelium.

Blocking macrophage recruitment or activation. CCL2–CCR2 blockade limits monocyte-derived macrophage recruitment and has been pursued in fibrosis, on the logic that interrupting the chemokine gradient severs the immune arm of the loop (12, 17). Modulating scar-associated macrophage activation offers a complementary lever, aiming to reorient rather than eliminate the niche's macrophages (4).

Targeting fibroblasts and intercellular signaling loops. Interfering with portal fibroblast and HSC activation—including their TGF-β- and PDGF-driven differentiation—directly targets the matrix-producing arm (24, 25). A complementary strategy is to disrupt key feed-forward interactions themselves: CCL2–CCR2, TGF-β (including αvβ6-mediated activation), PDGF, Hedgehog, and integrin-linked mechanotransduction represent candidate nodes that may weaken niche persistence (14, 15, 31, 32). Because several of these interactions are enriched or preferentially operative within the periductular microenvironment, spatially informed targeting may ultimately improve antifibrotic selectivity while preserving broader regenerative functions.

Spatially targeted therapies. Looking forward, the goal is not simply to deplete one cell type but to reshape the pathological spatial microenvironment—to restore a periductular milieu permissive to regeneration rather than fibrosis. Spatial omics-guided targeting of specific niche neighborhoods, rather than cell types, represents the conceptual frontier of this approach (5).

Outstanding questions and future directions
Several questions must be answered before this framework can be translated. First, when does the ductular reaction tip from regenerative response to pro-fibrotic driver, and what molecular switch determines that transition? Second, which cholangiocyte subpopulations constitute the true pathogenic population of the niche, and can they be distinguished from regenerative ones? Third, what are the relative contributions of portal fibroblasts versus hepatic stellate cells across different diseases and injury types? Fourth, is the spatial niche composition disease-specific, or does it converge on a common fibrogenic architecture? Fifth, can the fibrogenic niche be precisely disrupted without impairing the regenerative capacity essential for recovery? Answering these questions will require longitudinal, spatially resolved, and causally perturbed studies—not simply richer descriptive atlases.

Discussion
We propose a three-tiered reinterpretation of ductular reaction. First, it should not be regarded merely as a histological hallmark or a passive marker of disease activity. Second, it is a dynamic spatial niche maintained by epithelial–immune–mesenchymal interaction, in which reactive cholangiocytes, macrophages, and matrix-producing cells sustain one another through chemokines, TGF-β-centered signaling, ECM, and senescence. Third, this niche may represent the critical inflection point at which chronic injury shifts from regeneration to fibrosis—a transition whose control is of direct therapeutic relevance.

Several limitations temper this framework. Much of the spatial evidence derives from mouse models, and temporally resolved human data remain scarce; the field still lacks longitudinal maps that follow a single niche as it assembles, matures, and either resolves or becomes fixed. Niche composition likely differs across etiologies, and extrapolating from one disease to another—or from rodent to human—should be done cautiously. Most importantly, spatial correlation does not establish causation: co-localization of cell states does not by itself demonstrate directional, functional interaction.

Establishing causation will require perturbation studies—in organoid, co-culture, and in vivo systems—that selectively ablate or modulate one compartment of the niche and measure the response of the others, guided by the omics maps already available. Only such experiments can distinguish the causal nodes of the loop from its correlative correlates, and thereby identify which interactions are worth targeting therapeutically.

Conclusion
Ductular reaction is far more than the reactive proliferation of bile ductules. It is a spatially organized, self-sustaining fibrogenic niche assembled from reactive cholangiocytes, macrophages, and matrix-producing mesenchymal cells, held together by feed-forward signaling loops that span chemotaxis, TGF-β-centered fibrogenesis, matrix mechanics, and senescence.

Single-cell and spatial technologies now make this organization measurable and, increasingly, therapeutically addressable. Targeting the pathological organization of the ductular fibrogenic niche—rather than individual cell types alone—may provide a new therapeutic framework for chronic liver fibrosis, one that seeks to restore a regenerative microenvironment rather than merely to suppress its cellular inhabitants.

paper.title: Grouped but not unified: mechanistic diversity in mitochondrial skeletal disorders.
paper.abstract: Mitochondrial disease is a term assigned to a diverse group of genetic disorders caused by impaired mitochondrial function, resulting in defective oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthesis, with clinical manifestations that affect primarily energy-demanding tissues such as the brain and muscle. However, a subset of these conditions is characterized by prominent primary skeletal manifestations and has been designated Mitochondrial Skeletal disorders (MSDs). Since the initial review of MSDs in 2020, the number of genes in this category has expanded considerably, based on the updated Nosology of Genetic Skeletal disorders (2023) and MitoCarta3.0 (2021). In this review, we evaluate the clinical, genetic and functional evidence supporting the inclusion of the new genes and revisit the question of a shared mechanistic basis underlying this growing subgroup. Clinically, MSDs display pleiotropic and variable phenotypes, including dysplasia, craniofacial abnormalities and growth restriction. Functionally, the implicated proteins perform diverse essential roles in the mitochondria, extending beyond protein homeostasis to include maintenance of mtDNA integrity, mitochondrial metabolism, and membrane dynamics and composition. We hypothesize that these primary mitochondrial defects converge on the downstream activation of mitochondria-driven inflammatory pathways, disrupting osteogenic differentiation and bone formation through key signaling pathways (Wnt and Hedgehog), and transcription factors (RUNX2). However, consolidating this hypothesis will require deeper mechanistic studies using in vivo models, perturbation studies and multi-omic integration, ultimately enabling a more informed path towards the development of targeted therapeutic interventions.
