paper.title: The Role of METTL3-Mediated m(6)A Methylation in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Progression and Treatment.
paper.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a major cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide. Emerging evidence has established N6-methyladenosine (m6A) RNA methylation as a key epitranscriptomic mechanism underlying hepatocarcinogenesis. Methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3), the catalytic core of the m6A methyltransferase complex (MTC), forms a heterodimer with METTL14 and cooperates with auxiliary components of the MTC to deposit m6A modifications that modulate mRNA stability, splicing, nuclear export, and translation. In this review, we comprehensively summarize the current understanding of METTL3 biology in HCC, focusing on its structure, assembly within the MTC, regulation of coding and non-coding RNAs, and its roles in driving key oncogenic signaling cascades, such as JAK/STAT3, PI3K/AKT/mTOR, Wnt/β-catenin, Hippo/YAP, Notch, Hedgehog, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. In addition, we discussed how METTL3 remodels the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) by regulating immune responses and metabolic pathways promoting immune evasion and therapy resistance. Therapeutic strategies targeting METTL3-including small-molecule inhibitors, CRISPR-Cas9 approaches, combination immunotherapy, and tumor-selective delivery systems-are discussed together with the challenges that continue to limit clinical translation. Collectively, these findings position METTL3 as a central epitranscriptomic regulator of HCC progression; however, further mechanistic and clinical validation remains necessary to establish its utility as a therapeutic target and prognostic biomarker.
paper.full_text:
1. Introduction
Epitranscriptomics is the study of biochemical modifications on RNA molecules that regulate gene expression and RNA metabolic processes without altering the genetic sequence [1,2,3]. Numerous distinct RNA modifications have been identified to date, of which m6A is the most abundant and well-characterized modification in eukaryotic mRNA [4,5]. The m6A methylation functions as a dynamic and reversible epitranscriptomic regulatory mechanism, regulated by the interplay between “writers” (methyltransferases), “erasers” (demethylases), and “readers” (m6A-binding proteins) [6,7]. m6A is predominantly enriched within the 3′-untranslated regions (UTR) and near stop codons of mRNAs, where it regulates post-transcriptional gene regulation [1,5]. This modification regulates post-transcriptional processes, such as mRNA stability, alternative splicing, localization, translational efficiency, and cellular responses to oncogenic signaling [8,9,10]. Dysregulation of m6A homeostasis drives the initiation and progression of many cancers. Dysregulated m6A methylation disrupts the post-transcriptional stability and translation of oncogenic transcripts, resulting in broad transcriptomic alterations that promote cancer cell proliferation, metabolic reprogramming, immune evasion, and resistance to anticancer therapies, sustaining tumor growth [3,11,12,13]. In line with these findings, aberrant expression of m6A regulatory proteins is commonly observed in malignant tissues and is associated with advanced tumor stage, increased invasiveness, and poor patient survival [14].

Among the components of the m6A machinery, METTL3 functions as the principal catalytic writer and has attracted considerable attention in cancer research as it harbors the catalytic activity required for methyl-group transfer within the m6A MTC [13,15,16]. METTL3 constitutes the catalytic core of the MTC by forming a stable heterodimer with METTL14, which primarily facilitates RNA substrate recognition, whereas auxiliary proteins, including WTAP, VIRMA, RBM15/15B, ZC3H13, and HAKAI, govern complex assembly, subcellular localization, substrate selectivity, and methylation efficiency [3,17,18,19,20,21]. Using S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) as the universal methyl donor, the METTL3–METTL14 complex catalyzes m6A deposition on select target transcripts, enabling transcript-specific epitranscriptomic regulation upon recognition by m6A-binding proteins [2,16,22,23].

Although METTL3 has been implicated in a broad spectrum of malignancies, its biological role in hepatocarcinogenesis is context-dependent. Experimental evidence indicates that METTL3 exerts tumor-suppressive effects during the earliest stages of malignant transformation, whereas its oncogenic function predominates during established disease, depending on the transcript repertoire regulated, cellular state, and stage of hepatic tumor progression [24]. In HCC, aberrant METTL3 expression has been associated with altered regulation of oncogenic transcripts that drive tumor cell proliferation, metabolic adaptation, invasion, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance [11,13,25]. Elevated m6A modification has also been associated with resistance to chemotherapeutic agents and targeted therapies, including lenvatinib [26]. In addition to these tumor-intrinsic effects, METTL3 contributes to remodeling the tumor microenvironment (TME) by regulating immune and metabolic pathways, including impaired cytotoxic CD8+ T-cell infiltration and regulation of ferroptosis [9,27]. Yang et al. demonstrated that the HBXIP-METTL3 interaction contributes to HCC progression, suggesting METTL3 as a therapeutic target [28]. Taken together, these findings identify METTL3 as a key epitranscriptomic regulator in HCC and underscore its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target.

This review examines the molecular mechanisms through which METTL3-mediated m6A methylation drives HCC development and progression. Specifically, it addresses the structural organization and regulation of the m6A MTC, METTL3-dependent coding and non-coding RNA networks, oncogenic signaling, metabolic reprogramming, ferroptosis, and TIME, as well as current therapeutic strategies and the challenges associated with METTL3-targeted therapy.

For this review, relevant literature was identified through searches of PubMed, using combinations of the terms “METTL3,” “m6A,” “hepatocellular carcinoma,” and “HCC,” with emphasis on studies published up to August 2026.

2.1. Gene Structure and Protein Organization
The METTL3 gene encodes a modular protein comprising two principal functional domains: an N-terminal CCCH-type zinc finger domain (ZFD) and a C-terminal methyltransferase domain (MTD). These domains cooperate to ensure accurate substrate recognition and efficient m6A deposition [29,30,31]. The ZFD binds single-stranded RNA, contributing to substrate recognition by positioning target transcripts within the catalytic center. Although the ZFD lacks direct catalytic activity, this domain confers substrate specificity and facilitates efficient m6A deposition [30,32]. In contrast, the MTD harbors the conserved DPPW catalytic motif and the SAM-binding pocket, which cooperatively mediate methyl-group transfer to adenosine residues within the RRACH consensus sequence (R = A/G; H = A/C/U) (Figure 1) [29].

2.2.1. METTL3–METTL14 Heterodimer
The METTL3–METTL14 heterodimer constitutes the catalytic core of the m6A MTC. METTL3 provides catalytic activity [16], whereas METTL14 primarily serves as a structural scaffold that enhances RNA binding, stabilizes the heterodimer, and supports accurate m6A deposition [21,24,29,33,34,35]. Thus, RNA substrate recognition is cooperative: METTL14 provides the major RNA-binding interface and structural support, whereas the METTL3 ZFD contributes sequence-selective engagement and positioning of the target adenosine for catalysis. Additionally, the catalytic core is stabilized and regulated by several auxiliary proteins, including WTAP, VIRMA, RBM15/15B, ZC3H13, and HAKAI, which are essential for the regulation of complex localization and substrate selection of this complex, promoting its localization to nuclear speckles and directing the complex toward specific RNA substrates [2,15]. The MTD of METTL3 adopts a Rossmann fold architecture with gate loops that coordinate SAM binding and facilitate target adenosine recognition. METTL3 functions as the catalytic subunit of the m6A writer complex, while structural features of the METTL protein family, including N-terminal RNA-binding domains and C-terminal VCR motifs, modulate enzymatic efficiency in response to intracellular SAM availability [36,37]. The m6A landscape is reversible and tightly regulated by demethylases such as FTO and ALKBH5, which demethylate target transcripts and modulate m6A levels [38,39].

In HCC, increased METTL3 activity shifts the epitranscriptomic balance toward m6A hypermethylation, thereby stabilizing oncogenic transcripts and promoting tumor progression [40,41]. Recent studies have shown that METTL3 activity can also be regulated through post-translational modification. O-GlcNAcylation of METTL3 strengthens its interaction with WTAP, thereby increasing m6A methyltransferase activity and promoting HCC progression via MCM10 upregulation [22].

2.2.2. WTAP (Wilms’ Tumor 1-Associating Protein)
WTAP functions as a key regulatory and adaptor subunit that bridges the catalytic core of the MTC with auxiliary factors. By promoting the recruitment of the METTL3–METTL14 heterodimer to specific nuclear compartments, WTAP is required for ensuring the spatial organization and functional integrity of the complex [18,24,35,42]. WTAP is also essential for maintaining the structural integrity of the complex, as its depletion impairs the nuclear localization of METTL3 and METTL14 resulting in a global reduction in m6A levels [6,18].

In HCC, WTAP overexpression has been correlated with adverse clinicopathological features, including advanced tumor stage and poor survival outcomes [7,15]. Recent studies further demonstrate that WTAP drives HCC progression through selective m6A-dependent regulation of metabolic and ferroptosis-related transcripts. Under hypoxic conditions, WTAP-mediated m6A modification facilitates YTHDF2-mediated degradation of PPARGC1A mRNA, resulting in suppression of the PPARGC1A-BAMBI-ACSL5 axis. This pathway regulates Wnt/β-catenin and TGF-β/SMAD signaling, modulates reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, and regulates ferroptotic cell death, promoting HCC progression and lenvatinib resistance [27].

2.2.3. VIRMA
VIRMA, also known as KIAA1429, acts as a scaffold protein that recruits the MTC to a specific RNA region and cooperates with METTL3, METTL14, and WTAP to execute m6A methylation [42]. VIRMA directs the complex toward 3′-UTR and regions near stop codons, enabling site-selective m6A deposition [2,11].

In HCC, VIRMA promotes m6A modification of transcripts that support tumor cell proliferation and suppress apoptosis. VIRMA overexpression is associated with enhanced tumor aggressiveness and poor clinical outcomes through post-transcriptional regulation of oncogenic pathways [43,44]. Through its interaction with CPSF5 and CPSF6, VIRMA links the m6A MTC to the pre-mRNA 3′-end processing machinery, coupling m6A deposition with alternative polyadenylation and modulation of transcript stability. These mechanisms collectively promote the expression of VIRMA-regulated oncogenic transcripts and contribute to hepatocarcinogenesis [11].

2.2.4. RBM15/15B
RBM15 and RBM15B are RNA-binding proteins that bridge the association between the m6A MTC and target RNA substrates. By tethering the METTL3–METTL14 complex to specific motifs within nascent pre-mRNA, these proteins direct m6A deposition to defined RNA regions [11]. Specifically, RBM15 recognizes U-rich sequences and promotes m6A deposition on transcripts implicated in tumor cell proliferation and survival [4].

Recent studies have shown that RBM15 promotes METTL3-mediated m6A deposition on target transcripts, activating the IGF2BP1-YES1-MAPK signaling axis and driving HCC progression [33]. RBM15 modulates oncogenic signaling that sustains malignant progression, including increased tumor cell proliferation and survival.

2.2.5. ZC3H13
ZC3H13 is a zinc-finger protein that coordinates the nuclear localization and structural assembly of the m6A MTC. By retaining this complex within the nucleus, ZC3H13 promotes interactions among its subunits, optimizing the catalytic efficiency of the MTC [11]. ZC3H13 depletion impairs the functional integrity of the MTC in HCC, resulting in reduced m6A levels and impaired tumor cell proliferation. ZC3H13 also promotes malignancy by controlling the nuclear export of target transcripts, restricting METTL3-mediated m6A deposition to the nucleus to sustain oncogenic gene expression.

In addition to its role in MTC assembly, ZC3H13 is required for m6A-mediated post-transcriptional regulation of transcripts that drive proliferation and malignant progression in HCC [34]. Additionally, the interaction between MTC components and m6A reader YTHDF1 promotes metastatic progression through stabilization of oncogenic transcripts including FOXP4 [23].

2.2.6. HAKAI
HAKAI (also known as CBLL1) is an E3 ubiquitin ligase within the m6A MTC. It regulates the stability and turnover of the MTC, by controlling METTL3 protein levels required to maintain m6A homeostasis within the cell [11].

In HCC, HAKAI-mediated ubiquitination is a key regulatory mechanism; its dysregulation leads to aberrant METTL3 upregulation, which serves as an independent predictor of poor prognosis [36]. Thus, HAKAI acts as a regulatory component of the m6A MTC by controlling the abundance and activity of the methyltransferase complex rather than directly catalyzing m6A methylation.

2.3. Catalytic Mechanism of m6A
m6A deposition is governed by the coordinated activity of the MTC, which catalyzes methyl-group transfer to select adenosine residues within target transcripts [4]. This process occurs primarily in the nucleus and is closely coupled with transcription, enabling m6A deposition on nascent transcripts prior to RNA maturation. METTL3 preferentially methylates adenosine within the conserved RRACH consensus sequence [18,34,45]. Methyl-group transfer is mediated by SAM, which binds the catalytic pocket of METTL3 and donates a methyl group to the N6 position of the target adenosine. This reaction generates S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH) as a by-product [21,29]. Once deposited, m6A marks are recognized by reader proteins that regulate RNA stability, translation, and splicing, shaping transcript fate and gene expression [11].

3. METTL3-Mediated Molecular Mechanisms in HCC
Beyond its effects on protein-coding transcripts, METTL3 regulates multiple classes of coding and non-coding RNAs through m6A-dependent post-transcriptional mechanisms. These effects encompass mRNA stability and translation, microRNA (miRNA) biogenesis, long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) function, and circular RNA (circRNA) biogenesis, collectively broadening the post-transcriptional regulatory networks that drive HCC progression.

3.1.1. Regulation of mRNA Translation and Stability
Following m6A deposition, these modifications serve as post-transcriptional regulators of gene expression, modulating mRNA stability, and translational efficiency. The functional consequence of m6A is primarily determined by the recruitment of “reader” proteins, including members of the YTHDF family and IGF2BP3, which recognize m6A-modified sites to either promote transcript degradation or enhance transcript stability [17,46,47]. Whereas YTHDF proteins promote transcript decay, IGF2BP3 recognizes m6A-modified transcripts, stabilizing them, and enhancing their translation [17].

In HCC, this regulatory axis is commonly dysregulated, resulting in selective stabilization of oncogenic transcripts that promote tumor progression [41]. LIMA1 represents one such example whereby METTL3-mediated m6A modification stabilizes its mRNA, activating the Wnt/β-catenin and Hippo signaling pathways in HCC [10]. This mechanism similarly affects other drivers of HCC, such as FEN1 and EGFR, in which METTL3-driven transcript stabilization promotes aggressive proliferation and resistance to lenvatinib [13,26,48]. Collectively, these findings suggest that altered transcript stability via m6A modification is a key mechanism sustaining the malignant phenotype and driving chemoresistance in HCC cells [41].

Beyond its role in RNA stability and alternative splicing, m6A modification regulates translational efficiency by promoting the association of methylated transcripts with the translation machinery [17,46]. Reader proteins, including the YTHDF family members and IGF2BP3, bind m6A-modified transcripts, facilitate ribosome loading, and augment protein output from target transcripts [17,46,49]. In HCC, METTL3-mediated translational control sustains the expression of proteins implicated in tumor progression and therapeutic resistance. METTL3 enhances STAT3 translation, activating the JAK/STAT signaling pathway, while STAT3-driven WTAP upregulation may further promote METTL3 localization and MTC assembly (Figure 2) [15,17]. METTL3 also increases EGFR translation, driving lenvatinib resistance in HCC cells [26,48]. These findings demonstrate that dysregulated translational control represents a key mechanism by which METTL3 drives HCC progression and modulates therapeutic response.

3.1.2. Regulation of miRNAs
METTL3 regulates miRNA biogenesis through m6A-dependent processing of primary miRNAs (pri-miRNAs). m6A modification facilitates the recognition and processing of pri-miRNAs by the microprocessor complex, promoting the production of mature miRNAs [50,51]. In HCC, a recent study demonstrated that METTL3-mediated m6A modification of pri-miR-93 enhances its maturation into miR-93-5p, suppressing CDKN1A and promoting cell proliferation, cell-cycle progression, and resistance to apoptosis (Figure 3) [46]. A similar mechanism has been reported for miR-589-5p in liver cancer. METTL3 promotes miR-589-5p maturation through m6A modification of pri-miR-589, as METTL3 silencing increased pri-miR-589 levels while reducing mature miR-589-5p expression. Mutation of the identified m6A motif in pri-miR-589 further impaired miR-589-5p maturation, confirming the dependence of this process on m6A modification [52]. The METTL3/miR-589-5p axis also promoted liver cancer cell viability, migration, invasion, and xenograft tumor growth [52]. METTL3 can also affect miRNA activity indirectly through m6A modification of circRNAs. In HBV-associated HCC, METTL3 promoted the m6A-dependent biogenesis of circ-ARL3, which sponged miR-1305 and contributed to tumor progression [53]. METTL3 also regulated the m6A modification of circ-CCT3, which promoted HCC progression by sponging miR-378a-3p [54]. Together, these findings indicate that METTL3 regulates miRNA-mediated pathways in HCC through both direct control of miRNA maturation and indirect modulation of circRNA–miRNA interactions. However, evidence for METTL3-mediated regulation of miRNA pathways in HCC remains limited, while circRNA–miRNA interactions represent a potential direction for future investigation.

3.1.3. Regulation of Long Non-Coding RNAs (lncRNAs)
METTL3-mediated m6A modification regulates several oncogenic lncRNAs, including GBAP1, LINC00958, lnc-CTHCC, and MAPKAPK5-AS1 (MAAS), all of which promote HCC progression [55,56,57,58]. Among these, lncRNA GBAP1 is markedly overexpressed in HCC tissues [55]. METTL3 enhances GBAP1 expression and stability through m6A modification, promoting HCC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion via the miR-22-3p/BMPR1A/SMAD signaling pathway [55]. Similarly, METTL3 increases the stability of LINC00958 through m6A methylation, promoting lipogenesis through the miR-3619-5p/HDGF axis and enhancing HCC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion [58]. In addition, METTL3-mediated m6A modification of lnc-CTHCC is recognized by IGF2BP1 and IGF2BP3, which stabilize lnc-CTHCC and promote HCC growth and metastasis through the lnc-CTHCC/hnRNPK/YAP1 axis [57]. MAAS is another oncogenic lncRNA that is highly expressed in HCC tissues, and its elevated expression correlates with poor patient survival [56]. Furthermore, hepatitis B e antigen secreted by HCC cells promotes METTL3-mediated m6A modification, increasing MAAS expression in M2 macrophages. MAAS is subsequently transferred to HCC cells via M2 macrophage-derived exosomes, where it activates the MYC proto-oncogene to promote HCC cell proliferation [56].

3.1.4. Regulation of circRNAs
In HCC, some circRNAs function as oncogenic circRNAs, with high circRNA expression correlating with poor patient prognosis in HCC patients [53,54,59,60]. METTL3 regulates circRNA biogenesis through m6A-dependent modulation of back-splicing and promotes HCC progression by enhancing the expression and function of oncogenic circRNAs [59,61,62]. METTL3 increases the m6A modification of circ-CCT3, promoting HCC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion through the circ-CCT3/miR-378a-3p/FLT1 axis, representing a potential therapeutic target in HCC [54]. Similarly, HBx (hepatitis B virus X protein)-induced upregulation of METTL3 increases the m6A modification of circ-ARL3, recognized by the m6A reader YTHDC1, promoting its biogenesis, stability, and expression, disrupting the circ-ARL3/miR-1305 axis and facilitating HCC progression [53]. Likewise, METTL3-mediated m6A modification promotes the formation and accumulation of circHPS5, which is recognized by YTHDC1 facilitating its cytoplasmic export and activation of the circHPS5/miR-370/HMGA2 axis, promoting epithelial–mesenchymal transition, cancer stem-like properties, and HCC progression (Figure 4) [61]. Collectively, these findings identify METTL3-mediated m6A modification as a key regulator of oncogenic circRNA biogenesis in HCC.

3.2.1. JAK/STAT3 Feedback Signaling and Metastasis
A positive feedback loop between METTL3 and STAT3 has been identified in HCC [15,17]. METTL3-mediated m6A modification of STAT3 mRNA enhances its translation via YTHDF1-dependent recruitment of the translational initiation machinery, increasing STAT3 protein abundance [17]. STAT3 is a transcription factor that promotes HCC progression by regulating cellular proliferation, survival, angiogenesis, and metastatic dissemination [15]. In turn, STAT3 transcriptionally upregulates WTAP, a core component of the MTC, facilitating METTL3 nuclear translocation and enhancing overall m6A methyltransferase activity [17]. This METTL3–STAT3 positive feedback loop amplifies oncogenic signaling and drives HCC metastasis in both in vitro and in vivo models [15,17].

3.2.2. EGFR/PI3K/AKT/mTOR
METTL3 enhances EGFR/PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling through m6A-mediated post-transcriptional regulation [8,33]. The EGFR/PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling axis drives oncogenic phenotypes including uncontrolled proliferation, anabolic metabolism, survival, migration, and resistance to apoptosis [33,63,64]. It also shapes the TME regulation by promoting angiogenesis and inflammatory cell recruitment. METTL3 marks PTEN and TSC2 mRNAs for YTHDF2-mediated degradation, relieving two negative regulators of the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis and driving sustained pathway activation [8,33]. METTL3 also promotes metabolic reprogramming to support malignant cell survival. METTL3-mediated m6A modification targets the 3′-UTR of TRIM21 mRNA, promoting its YTHDF2-dependent destabilization. This event prevents TRIM21-mediated ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation of G6PD, indicating that METTL3 stabilizes G6PD by impairing TRIM21-mediated proteasomal degradation [8,65]. G6PD stabilization significantly elevates the pentose phosphate pathway flux, generating the necessary NADPH and nucleotide precursors to facilitate tumor growth and confer resistance to platinum-based chemotherapies, such as oxaliplatin, as well as tyrosine kinase inhibitors like lenvatinib [8,48]. METTL3-mediated m6A modification of transcripts encoding serine synthesis pathway (SSP) enzymes, through an IGF2BP3-dependent stabilization mechanism, promotes activation of this metabolic axis in sorafenib-resistant HCC cells [66,67]. Activation of the m6A-SSP axis increases intracellular antioxidant capacity, reduces ROS levels, and promotes tumor cell survival under sorafenib-induced stress, contributing to METTL3-associated therapeutic resistance [67].

3.2.3. Wnt/β-Catenin
METTL3 promotes Wnt/β-catenin signaling in HCC through m6A-dependent upregulation of the Frizzled receptor FZD10, a Wnt receptor [3,68]. Hyperactivation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling axis occurs in approximately 20–40% of HCCs and contributes to tumor stemness, proliferation, and drug resistance [69]. Wang et al. showed that m6A modification of FZD10 mRNA enhances its stability and translation, increasing Wnt pathway activation (Figure 5) [68]. Enhanced Wnt signaling promotes cancer stem cell properties, lenvatinib resistance, and YAP activation in HCC [1,10]. These findings indicate that METTL3 coordinates Wnt/β-catenin and Hippo/YAP signaling through interconnected oncogenic mechanisms in HCC [8]. METTL3 upregulation is also associated with lenvatinib resistance in HCC and has been proposed as a biomarker for predicting therapeutic response [36].

3.2.4. Hippo/YAP Signaling
METTL3-mediated m6A modification modulates the activity of the Hippo/YAP pathway, a pathway that regulates tumor growth and liver regeneration [8,70]. Transcriptomic analysis following METTL3 knockdown revealed significant enrichment of the Hippo pathway, while m6A profiling revealed that YAP1 mRNA is a direct target of METTL3 [70]. In addition to directly modifying YAP1 mRNA, METTL3 also activates Hippo/YAP signaling by regulating MOB1A mRNA. METTL3 promotes YTHDF2-mediated decay of MOB1A, a core component of the Hippo kinase cascade, reducing inhibitory YAP phosphorylation and promoting its nuclear accumulation to drive pro-tumorigenic transcriptional programs associated with hepatocarcinogenesis [8,70]. Loss of MOB1A disrupts canonical Hippo inhibitory signaling and promotes proliferation, survival, and stemness-associated phenotypes in aggressive HCC [70]. Activated YAP also cooperates with the Wnt/β-catenin pathway to further promote HCC progression. The crosstalk supports cancer stem cell properties and therapeutic resistance [3,10].

3.2.5. EMT-Associated Pathways
Elevated METTL3 expression is associated with an enhanced epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) in HCC, promoting invasive and migratory characteristics that facilitate metastatic dissemination [71,72,73]. METTL3 mediates this effect through m6A-dependent post-transcriptional regulation of key EMT-promoting transcription factors and signaling mediators. For example, METTL3-mediated m6A modification stabilizes IQGAP3 mRNA through IGF2BP2-dependent recognition, activating TGF-β/SMAD signaling and inducing EMT, which promotes HCC cell migration, invasion, and metastasis in vitro and in vivo [71]. By increasing the stability and translational efficiency of these pro-metastatic transcripts, METTL3 promotes cellular invasion, extracellular matrix remodeling, and metastatic progression [74,75]. In gastric cancer, METTL3-mediated stabilization of transcripts such as ZMYM1 facilitates EMT, suggesting a conserved mechanism across cancer types [32,76]. In cholangiocarcinoma, METTL3-dependent modulation of alternative pathways, including YTHDF2-mediated degradation of IFIT2 mRNA, also promotes tumor progression [77]. Together, these findings suggest that METTL3 promotes EMT and metastatic progression across hepatic and gastrointestinal malignancies, although the downstream effectors differ among tumor types.

3.2.6. Notch Signaling
The Notch signaling pathway is a highly conserved intercellular communication cascade that regulates essential cellular processes through interactions between neighboring cells. Abnormal activation of Notch signaling has been widely implicated in HCC, where it promotes tumor initiation and progression by enhancing cell proliferation, metastasis, stem cell-like properties, and resistance to anticancer therapies [78]. In contrast, DLL3 has been reported to negatively regulate HCC cell growth by suppressing Notch signaling, although its expression is frequently silenced through promoter methylation in human HCC [79]. Consistent with the oncogenic role of Notch signaling, Wu et al. reported that high METTL3 expression in HCC tissues positively correlated with activation of the Wnt, cell cycle, and Notch signaling pathways [40]. Downstream, the YTHDF1–NOTCH1 axis directly contributes to therapeutic resistance in HCC. YTHDF1 binds to m6A-modified NOTCH1 mRNA, enhancing its stability and translational efficiency, which increases tumor-initiating capacity and self-renewal. Depletion of YTHDF1 increases the sensitivity of HCC cells to lenvatinib and sorafenib, whereas enforced expression of NOTCH1 promotes resistance to these therapies [80]. Notch1 activation also promotes EMT in HCC, facilitating stem cell-like properties, migration, invasion, and chemoresistance. These observations highlight the crosstalk between Notch signaling and other oncogenic pathways in HCC [81].

3.2.7. Hedgehog Signaling
The Hedgehog signaling pathway is aberrantly activated in a subset of HCCs and contributes to cancer stem cell maintenance, epithelial–mesenchymal transition, and therapeutic resistance [74,82]. However, the direct contribution of METTL3-mediated m6A regulation to Hedgehog activation in HCC remains incompletely defined. Studies in other cancer models have shown that METTL3 can regulate Hedgehog pathway activity through m6A-dependent post-transcriptional mechanisms. In the Sonic Hedgehog subgroup of medulloblastoma, METTL3-mediated m6A modification of PTCH1 and GLI2 transcripts enhances their RNA stability and translation, activating Sonic Hedgehog signaling and promoting tumor progression [83]. In HCC, hypoxia-driven ROS-mediated non-canonical Hedgehog signaling has been implicated in EMT and may contribute to tumor progression and therapeutic resistance [72,84]. Whether a similar METTL3-dependent regulatory mechanism contributes to Hedgehog activation in HCC remains to be established.

3.3. Cellular Reprogramming in HCC
In addition to regulating oncogenic signaling pathways, METTL3 also influences several cellular processes that contribute to HCC progression. METTL3-mediated m6A modification regulates cell cycle progression, glycolytic reprogramming, autophagy, and immune evasion, enabling HCC cells to sustain proliferation under metabolic and therapeutic stress. METTL3 promotes G1/S cell cycle progression by enhancing the stability and translation of cell cycle-related mRNAs [49], while also increasing glycolytic activity through the regulation of enzymes and metabolic factors involved in aerobic glycolysis, providing the energy and biosynthetic intermediates required for continuous proliferation [28]. The increased metabolic demand of this proliferative state is offset by METTL3-dependent regulation of autophagy, which preserves cellular homeostasis by recycling intracellular components during nutrient deprivation, hypoxia, and treatment-induced stress. In HCC, persistent activation of autophagy has also been linked to improved tumor cell survival and reduced sensitivity to therapies such as sorafenib [47,85]. METTL3 also influences TIME by regulating immune checkpoint molecules and other immunomodulatory factors, suppressing antitumor immune responses, and facilitating immune escape [25,86]. Collectively, these mechanisms sustain tumor growth and reduce therapeutic sensitivity in HCC.

3.4.1. Cytokine Regulation
METTL3 regulates cytokine signaling primarily through the SOCS/JAK/STAT axis. METTL3 forms a positive feedback loop with STAT3, a transcription factor activated downstream of cytokine signaling, while SOCS2 and SOCS3 function as negative regulators of this pathway by limiting cellular sensitivity to cytokine-driven growth signals [15,25,87,88]. Sustained STAT3 activity promotes transcriptional programs associated with tumor cell survival, metabolic adaptation, and oncogenic cytokine signaling [8]. METTL3-mediated m6A modification facilitates YTHDF2-dependent decay of SOCS2 mRNA in HCC [25,33], impairing a negative regulatory mechanism that normally constrains JAK/STAT pathway activation and sustaining STAT3-dependent transcription [15]. In HCC, METTL3 overexpression promotes YTHDF2-dependent degradation of SOCS2 mRNA, reducing SOCS2 expression and enhancing HCC cell proliferation and migration through aberrant STAT3 signaling [8,25,89].

3.4.2. T-Cell Dysfunction
METTL3 contributes to T-cell dysfunction by remodeling the TME [90,91]. Activation of oncogenic pathways, such as the JAK/STAT signaling, disrupts normal immune surveillance [88,91]. The resulting metabolic and signaling changes promote an immunosuppressive microenvironment that limits antitumor immune responses in HCC. One mechanism involves METTL3-dependent m6A modification of SREBP cleavage-activating protein (SCAP), enhancing cholesterol biosynthesis, and impairing the anti-tumor activity of CD8+ T cells, contributing to resistance to immune checkpoint blockade [9,91]. METTL3 has been implicated in HCC immune evasion through the SMPDL3A/LRPPRC axis. METTL3-mediated m6A modification stabilizes SMPDL3A mRNA, thereby increasing LRPPRC expression and promoting HCC-associated immune escape [41]. In a separate HCC study, LRPPRC was shown to interact with PD-L1 mRNA and enhance its m6A-dependent stability; accordingly, LRPPRC depletion reduced PD-L1 mRNA and protein expression and enhanced antitumor immunity [92]. These findings suggest a possible indirect link between METTL3 and PD-L1 regulation; however, the cited studies do not establish direct METTL3-mediated m6A modification of PD-L1 mRNA in HCC. Taken together, the studies discussed above support a role for METTL3 in shaping the immune microenvironment of HCC.

Collectively, METTL3 regulates diverse coding and non-coding RNA targets, oncogenic signaling pathways, metabolic programs, and immune responses in HCC, as summarized in Table 1.

4. Therapeutic Strategies Targeting METTL3 in HCC
METTL3 overexpression across multiple cancer types and its strong correlation with poor prognosis make it an attractive therapeutic target [4,15]. Moreover, METTL3-mediated m6A modifications have been implicated in drug resistance. However, therapeutic strategies must account for METTL3’s context-dependent roles, as its silencing may paradoxically promote sorafenib resistance through autophagy-related pathways [8].

4.1. Small-Molecule and Peptide-Based Inhibition of METTL3
HCC treatment has been substantially advanced by the introduction of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), which target key regulatory pathways such as CTLA-4 and PD-1/PD-L1. These therapies have transformed treatment paradigms and demonstrated clinical efficacy in HCC [91]. However, despite these successes, limitations such as variable response and acquired resistance have driven the search for complementary therapeutic strategies. Targeting epitranscriptomic regulators such as METTL3 represents a potential therapeutic strategy. The initial discovery of METTL3 inhibitors stemmed from high-throughput screening of adenosine analogues, designed to bind the SAM binding site and inhibit methyltransferase activity [96]. Based on the crystal structure of the METTL3 catalytic pocket, recent drug development efforts have focused on SAM-competitive inhibitors that specifically target the MTD of METTL3. By mimicking the SAM cofactor, these inhibitors disrupt the catalytic activity of the METTL3–METTL14 complex enhancing selectivity and minimizing off-target interactions with other methyltransferases. Despite ongoing challenges in pharmacokinetic optimization, this rational design strategy represents a significant step toward the precise epitranscriptomic modulation in METTL3-driven HCC [36].

Although preclinical data are promising, the clinical translation of METTL3-targeted therapies, such as STC-15, remains in its early stages, with no established HCC-specific clinical efficacy data to date [13,36,95]. In Phase I (NCT05584111), STC-15 achieved target engagement and showed preliminary antitumor activity in 42 patients with advanced malignancies. The ongoing Phase 1b/2 trial (NCT06975293), evaluating STC-15 in combination with the anti-PD-1 antibody toripalimab, has an estimated enrollment of 107 participants [91,97,98]. However, HCC-specific clinical efficacy has not been established, and these findings cannot yet be directly extrapolated to HCC.

Several selective METTL3 inhibitors, including STC-15, UZH1a, and STM2457, have been developed, with some progressing into early-phase clinical trials although translating these preclinical findings into clinical practice remains challenging [6,36]. Most evidence is derived from preclinical studies, and clinical validation of safety, efficacy, and delivery strategies remains necessary [6]. Alongside small-molecule inhibitors, peptide-based strategies are being developed to disrupt METTL3 protein–protein interactions, potentially reducing immunogenicity and limiting acquired resistance [22,32,99]. Among these inhibitors, STC-15 has demonstrated both antitumor and immunomodulatory activities [100,101]. Preclinical studies indicate that STC-15 activates innate immune signaling and enhances the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors, including anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-1/PD-L1 antibodies [91,100,101,102]. This approach may help overcome the limitations of monotherapy and improve therapeutic outcomes in HCC, supporting a potential role for METTL3 inhibition in combination immunotherapy strategies [6,9].

Similarly, the small-molecule inhibitor STM2457 has demonstrated antitumor activity and immunomodulatory effects in preclinical models. By binding to the catalytic domain of METTL3, STM2457 selectively inhibits its methyltransferase activity, reducing global m6A methylation. Consequently, STM2457 suppresses cell viability [65], proliferation (as indicated by decreased EdU-positive cells) [41], and invasion, while promoting apoptosis in vitro and in vivo models [26,36]. Jin et al. reported that STM2457 enhanced HCC cell sensitivity to oxaliplatin and demonstrated that the METTL3/TRIM21/G6PD axis contributes to oxaliplatin resistance, supporting METTL3 inhibition as a potential strategy for overcoming chemoresistance [65]. STM2457 has also been reported to reverse lenvatinib resistance, collectively supporting METTL3 inhibition as a strategy to overcome drug resistance in HCC [26,36]. Furthermore, combining STM2457 with sorafenib improved therapeutic responsiveness by disrupting METTL3-driven activation of the serine synthesis pathway and impairing the metabolic and antioxidant adaptation of resistant HCC cells [67]. Collectively, these findings support METTL3 inhibition, either alone or in combination with existing therapies, as a promising strategy for overcoming drug resistance in HCC.

4.2. CRISPR-Cas9-Based Strategies
Studies using METTL3 knock-in, CRISPR-Cas9 knockout, and knockdown approaches have established METTL3 as a critical regulator of tumor cell survival, particularly in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)-associated HCC [9]. These studies consistently demonstrate that METTL3 ablation attenuates tumor cell proliferation, survival, and metastatic potential [4,9,24]. Although METTL3 ablation suppresses tumor progression in most models, enhanced hepatocarcinogenesis has been reported in specific contexts, indicating context-dependent roles of METTL3 [24]. This functional divergence suggests that METTL3 can assume protective roles under specific conditions, as evidenced by its modulation of adaptive autophagy pathways. METTL3 silencing may activate protective autophagy that promotes sorafenib resistance [8], potentially limiting the efficacy of METTL3-targeted therapies. Collectively, these findings indicate that the therapeutic effects of METTL3 inhibition are context dependent, necessitating consideration of tumor-specific dependencies and resistance mechanisms in therapeutic development.

4.3. Combination Immunotherapy in HCC
METTL3 modulation may enhance the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade. Targeting METTL3 has been shown to synergize with anti-PD-1 therapy, leading to robust tumor growth inhibition, including >90% reductions in tumor volume and weight compared with the control, by reinvigorating CD8+ T-cell function and alleviating the immunosuppressive microenvironment [9,91]. Characterizing the regulatory crosstalk between METTL3 and immune checkpoints such as PD-L1 offers a compelling rationale for incorporating epitranscriptomic-targeted therapies into combination regimens to counteract immune evasion in HCC [5]. Therapeutic strategies targeting the METTL3–METTL14 complex are being developed to disrupt m6A-dependent oncogenic signaling. In addition to conventional catalytic inhibition, emerging strategies such as PROTAC-mediated degradation, exemplified by WD6305, aim to eliminate the methyltransferase machinery through targeted protein degradation. This approach may offer advantages over conventional enzymatic inhibition by achieving more complete suppression of METTL3 activity [103,104].

4.4. Delivery Systems Targeting Liver Tumors
Efficient drug delivery remains a critical bottleneck for the clinical translation of METTL3-targeted therapies in HCC [6]. The therapeutic utility of small-molecule METTL3 inhibitors is often limited by poor water solubility, low bioavailability, and potential systemic off-target toxicity [48]. To overcome these challenges, future research must focus on optimizing advanced delivery systems, including nanoparticle-based carriers, to achieve tumor-selective delivery within the hepatic TME while minimizing systemic toxicity [6,48]. Approaches like the use of ligand-conjugated or stimulus-responsive nanoparticles have demonstrated potential to enhance drug stability, improve tumor penetration, and facilitate controlled release within the TME [48]. Furthermore, nanoparticle-based delivery of genetic agents such as siMETTL3 has demonstrated robust antitumor immune responses and improved efficacy in combination with immunotherapy in preclinical models [9,48].

5. Current Challenges and Future Perspectives
Despite substantial evidence supporting METTL3 as an important regulator of HCC progression, several challenges remain before METTL3-directed strategies can be translated into clinically effective therapies. Key issues include the context-dependent functions of METTL3, patient selection, biomarker development, treatment resistance and potential on-target toxicity, and the limited clinical validation of METTL3-targeted therapies.

The role of METTL3 may differ across the cellular and molecular contexts and stages of hepatocarcinogenesis. Experimental evidence suggests that METTL3 may exert tumor-suppressive effects during early hepatocarcinogenesis, in contrast to its previously reported oncogenic role in established HCC [24]. Therefore, the effects of METTL3 inhibition may depend on the stage of tumor development. In addition, METTL3 activity may differ between malignant hepatocytes and immune or stromal cells within the tumor microenvironment. Thus, METTL3 expression measured in bulk tumor tissue may not fully reflect METTL3 dependency in malignant cells [4,5,91].

Reliable biomarkers are also needed for patient selection, prognosis, and therapeutic monitoring [13,107]. Clinical evidence supports a role for METTL3 in HCC progression, prognosis, and therapeutic resistance. METTL3 was significantly upregulated in 50 paired HCC and normal liver tissues. In the same study, an analysis of 360 HCC patients using TCGA and cBioPortal data identified METTL3 expression as an independent prognostic factor for overall survival (multivariate HR = 2.046, 95% CI: 1.303–3.212, p = 0.002) and recurrence-free survival [20]. In an independent analysis of 10 paired HCC and adjacent non-tumor tissues, METTL3 and STAT3 protein levels were significantly elevated in HCC tissues, particularly in metastatic lesions. Analysis of tissue microarrays comprising 122 clinical specimens further demonstrated a strong positive correlation between METTL3 and STAT3 protein expression (r = 0.656, p < 0.001), while functional studies showed that the METTL3–STAT3–WTAP positive-feedback loop promoted HCC metastasis [15]. In a cohort of 74 HCC patients receiving adjuvant lenvatinib after radical treatment, high METTL3 expression was associated with poorer overall survival (37 patients each in the high- and low-expression groups). METTL3 expression was also higher in lenvatinib-resistant than in lenvatinib-sensitive HCC tissues. In preclinical models, METTL3 inhibition with STM2457 enhanced lenvatinib sensitivity by suppressing EGFR translation [26]. These findings support the prognostic and therapeutic potential of METTL3, although its predictive value for METTL3-targeted therapy remains unclear. Circulating m6A-related markers may also have monitoring potential but require prospective validation [74,107].

Therapeutic resistance and toxicity remain additional concerns. METTL3-mediated m6A regulation has been implicated in resistance to therapies such as sorafenib, highlighting the need to understand acquired resistance and develop rational combination strategies [64,85,108]. Meanwhile, because METTL3 also regulates physiological processes such as hepatic lipid metabolism, systemic inhibition may affect normal liver function. Poor drug bioavailability and limited target specificity may further restrict clinical translation, emphasizing the need for an adequate therapeutic window and improved tumor selectivity [13,108].

Several therapeutic strategies targeting METTL3, including selective small-molecule inhibitors and approaches that disrupt MTC function, have demonstrated promising preclinical activity. However, improving target specificity, establishing long-term safety, and achieving tumor-selective delivery remain important priorities for clinical development. Rational combination strategies with established targeted therapies or immunotherapies may also improve therapeutic efficacy while limiting systemic effects [6,109].

Future studies should integrate multi-omics, single-cell, and spatial approaches with improved preclinical models to delineate the molecular determinants governing METTL3 activity across distinct cellular populations within the HCC microenvironment, identify predictive biomarkers, and clarify resistance mechanisms [4,9,74,108]. From a therapeutic perspective, more selective METTL3 inhibitors and targeted delivery strategies could be explored in combination with immunotherapy, radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or established targeted therapies such as sorafenib [109]. Prospective HCC trials with appropriate biomarker stratification, pharmacodynamic assessment, and long-term safety evaluation are needed to determine the clinical benefit of METTL3-targeted therapy [13,36]. The overarching connections between METTL3-mediated RNA regulation, oncogenic signaling, immune microenvironment remodeling, and targeted therapeutic strategies discussed in this review are summarized in Figure 6.

6. Conclusions
METTL3 has emerged as a central regulator of m6A RNA methylation, playing a pivotal role in the development and progression of HCC. Through post-transcriptional regulation of both coding and non-coding RNAs, METTL3 orchestrates multiple biological processes, including oncogenic signaling, RNA metabolism, metabolic reprogramming, immune evasion, and therapeutic response. Collectively, these diverse functions position METTL3 at the nexus of the epitranscriptomic networks that drive HCC progression, supporting its value as both a prognostic biomarker and a therapeutic target.

Accumulating evidence supports METTL3 as a promising therapeutic target, with selective small-molecule inhibitors and approaches targeting the MTC demonstrating encouraging preclinical activity. However, the context-dependent functions of METTL3, together with challenges related to patient selection, target specificity, therapeutic resistance, and long-term safety, remain important considerations for clinical translation. Although METTL3 inhibitors have entered early clinical evaluation, their clinical efficacy in HCC remains to be established.

Overall, further integration of mechanistic, epitranscriptomic, and clinical studies will be required to define the therapeutic potential of METTL3 in HCC. Such efforts may support the development of more precise METTL3-targeted strategies and identify patients most likely to benefit from these approaches.
